tracks.title: The talk outruns the build
tracks.text: Lesson 04 point 8 — claims. This one is a sub-lesson, under org… the grammar. And it is the sharpest argument that grammar makes. Here is the problem. Founder speech is the densest spec a company ever produces. The 91-minute voice memo on the drive home… the pitch paced around the kitchen… the meeting where the whole architecture finally clicked out loud. That is the product, described by the one person who holds all of it at once. And it all rots — identically — in a notes app, as a transcript nobody re-reads. [sighs] But here is the worse part. The talk always outruns the build. Every founder ships sentences before they ship systems. You describe the thing you mean to make, in the present tense, long before it exists. And that's fine… until nobody is tracking which sentences are still fiction. The gap between the spoken system and the shipped system is invisible — right up until a buyer, or a security review, finds it for you, and names it in the room.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: So — the definition. A claim is a load-bearing spoken assertion, extracted from an untouched source as an org TODO item, whose state is its honesty. It moves from CLAIMED toward a verdict… and it reaches a terminal state only with cited evidence — a file, an epic, a test, or a live run. [curious] And the move hiding in that definition is the whole lesson. A transcript is a source… not a document. The working document is the ledger you derive from it. And because org lets you declare your own TODO keyword ladder in a single line, that derived document can make honesty itself into a state machine — the same TODO-to-DONE you already trust… with a conscience bolted on.

tracks.title: Seven words of state machine
tracks.text: Now — seven words of state machine. This is the entire mechanism. One line, at the top of the audit file, declares a custom keyword ladder. It reads — hash plus TODO, colon — CLAIMED, VALIDATING… then a pipe… then KEPT, PARTIAL, UNKEPT, FUTURE, RETRACTED. [excited] That pipe is the spine. Left of it are the two working states — a claim still in flight. Right of it are the five verdicts — terminal, and each one forbidden without a citation. Now picture the machine those seven words describe. A claim enters at CLAIMED, and it can only leave for VALIDATING — being checked against the actual repo. From VALIDATING there are five exits. First… KEPT, for what is true. Second… PARTIAL, for what is half true. Third… UNKEPT, for what was said but never built. Fourth… FUTURE, for what you deliberately have not built yet. And fifth… RETRACTED, for a claim that turned out plain wrong. And over the whole branch hangs one rule — no claim crosses into any verdict without dragging evidence across with it. A cited file, epic, test, or run. The seven words are the same shape as TODO-to-DONE — only here, reaching DONE means you proved something.

tracks.title: Quote, then evidence
tracks.text: Next — quote, then evidence. A claim entry has a fixed anatomy, and the discipline lives in keeping its two halves in two different voices. The headline carries the status, and the claim, as one sentence. The body carries a Quote — the verbatim words from the source, never paraphrased — and then a Reality line — what is actually true in the repo. Let me read you a real one. The headline — KEPT — a workbook is an HTML file. The quote, the founder's own words — if you looked at a workbook, you would at first glance see an HTML file… natively zipped… a SQLite binary file. And then the evidence, the repo answering — the authoring surface ships single-file dot-HTML mini-apps, bundling a WASM runtime, SQLite, and their own source. [curious] Hear what just happened. One voice is what was said. The other is what is. And they are allowed to disagree — that disagreement is the entire point of the document — so they must never be written by the same hand, in the same breath. Which is why the verbatim rule isn't pedantry. The moment you paraphrase the quote, you quietly edit the claim toward the version you can defend… and the audit becomes a record of what you wish you had said.

tracks.title: The five verdicts
tracks.text: Now a closer look at the right-hand side — the five verdicts, each with a real specimen from the one live audit. First… KEPT — compilers run inside the sandbox, C, Zig, Rust, Go, and JavaScript. Cited reality — epic done, the compilers package shipped, recipes in the tree. Second… PARTIAL — bash is emulated in WebAssembly, no native exec anywhere. Reality — the emulated shape exists and the no-native-exec rule holds, but a hardened interim real-exec tool still does too, with an epic open to remove it. Half true. Third… UNKEPT — most of Python compiles and runs in the sandbox. Reality — there is no Python lane at all. Build it, or stop saying it. Fourth… FUTURE — a non-LLM model trained on runtime telemetry diffuses changes into the engine. Reality — deliberately unbuilt, named and parked as direction, not pretended as shipped. And fifth… RETRACTED — Erlang gives nine-nines fault tolerance. Reality — that's folklore from one old anecdote, widely contested. Drop the number… keep the true supervision-tree story. [chuckles] And those last two are the ones that earn the whole discipline. The Python line sounds true because the sentence next to it is true. And the nine-nines line isn't half-built — it's just wrong. An audit is the only thing that catches either one before a customer does.

tracks.title: Audio in, ledger out
tracks.text: Next — audio in, ledger out. The ledger is the end of a pipeline, and every step of it is agent-runnable — which is exactly why the whole method is a candidate toolkit. Follow the path that produced the one live audit. It starts with a 91-minute voice memo — 5,454 seconds. That goes through ElevenLabs scribe, and lands as two untouched files in a dated source folder. First… verbatim dot text — exactly 8,578 words. Second… words dot JSON — every single word, with its start time, its end time, and the model's confidence. The transcript knows not just what was said… but when, and how sure it was. From those sources the audit is derived — and the audit's source line points right back at them. The sources are never edited. The audit is the only thing that changes. And the final step on the right is the payoff — every UNKEPT and every PARTIAL falls straight into a backlog. [curious] And that append-only rule on the sources is what makes it trustworthy over time. Re-audit the same memo a year from now, and the words you are checking against have not drifted. The document moves. The truth it was built from does not.

tracks.title: The gap is the backlog
tracks.text: Now the thesis the audit states about itself, word for word — the gap between the spoken system and the shipped system is the backlog. [excited] An UNKEPT is not a confession. It is a ticket. And the method doesn't stop at judging — it dispatches. Picture the loop that actually runs on this project, as a hand-off between five players. First, the founder, on a live call, names a claim that worries him — in the real file, workbook-as-container, flagged as the weakest pitch line. Second, the groundskeeper agent saves that thought to a dated capture file. Third, it hands a research goal to an author model — Mercury 2 — which writes the goal up as an org TODO outline, where every leaf carries a done-when shell gate that has to pass. Fourth, the run executes, and its results land on the task ledger — generated from the runtime, never hand-edited. And fifth… the next call picks up right where this one left off. And the loop closes hardest on the scariest claim in the whole audit — thousands of agents per server, insanely high concurrency — whose cited reality is brutal. The first live co-tenant run overloaded a four-agent box. So on a real archived call, the founder turned that worry into work, by voice, in one sentence — file an issue, titled load benchmark for concurrent agents. We claim thousands of agents per server with no proof… build a benchmark. And the agent answered — issue filed. One claim… one verdict still pending… one benchmark now on the backlog. The method, end to end, just by talking.

tracks.title: A ledger you can grep
tracks.text: Here's a small one that does a lot — a ledger you can grep. Because every status is a headline keyword in a plain text file, the health of your pitch is one shell command away. You don't need a dashboard. You need grep. Count the UNKEPTs — there is one. Count the still-unchecked CLAIMEDs — there are six. And tally the whole ladder at once — KEPT seven… PARTIAL three… CLAIMED six… UNKEPT one… FUTURE one. [curious] Those are the real counts from the one live ledger. And they tell you something the prose can't — this audit is ahead of its own data. The ladder declares RETRACTED and VALIDATING… yet neither has a single live instance. Six claims still sit unchecked. The retraction of the nine-nines line has been argued for, but not yet stamped. And that is honest — grep is what makes it visible. Pitch health becomes arithmetic… legible to a human, an agent, and a one-line script, all at the same time.

tracks.title: More than a checklist
tracks.text: One more, before the honest part — it's more than a checklist. A claims audit is not just a column of verdicts. The same pass over a single 91-minute ramble extracts a full working document. First… the argument skeleton — the pitch rebuilt as a numbered structure, the spine the claims hang on. Second… the audiences — who each part of the talk is actually for. Third… the contrast objects — the named competitors and foils. And fourth… the open questions — the dangling threads the founder left unresolved out loud. [excited] So one unscripted ramble, run through this method, yields a checked claims ledger, a positioning map, a competitor list, and a question backlog. A working document — not a checklist. The transcript was never the deliverable. The audit is.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where it bites. And a claims lesson that hid its own UNKEPTs would be a bad joke. Four places this bites. First… status is judgment, not proof. A human or an agent reads the repo and decides KEPT or PARTIAL. The evidence rule constrains that judgment — it does not automate it. A generous auditor can still stamp KEPT on a half-truth. Second… KEPT rots. Evidence ages. A claim that was true against last quarter's repo can quietly go stale, and a verdict carries no expiry date. Third — and this one is precise — the runtime can't execute this exact ladder yet. The workflow engine reads a file's own TODO line… but its parser does not strip the Emacs fast-selection keys. It reads KEPT-paren-k as one token, so a headline stamped KEPT matches nothing, and parses as no state at all. Emacs strips that paren. Our runtime parser doesn't. So today the ladder is fully readable by humans, agents, and grep — but it is not executable workflow state in the engine. And fourth… n equals one. One memo has been audited this way. And the drift validator this method implies — a checker that flags a verdict with no evidence behind it — does not exist yet. [sighs] The method's sharpest promise is one of its own UNKEPT items. And we would rather tell you that… than imply otherwise.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Isn't this just fact-checking the pitch? No. Fact-checking ends at a verdict column. This doesn't. The verdicts feed a backlog — an UNKEPT is a ticket, not a scarlet letter. The output isn't a grade. It's work. Who assigns the status? Whoever can cite evidence — human or agent, it doesn't matter. The rule isn't about authority… it's about the citation. Why org, and not a spreadsheet? Because the ladder lives in the same grammar as the workflows it spawns. A spreadsheet would make the audit a fifth system of record — the exact fragmentation org is here to end. Can I retract a KEPT? Yes — and you should, when evidence ages. A verdict is a snapshot of a moment, not a permanent ruling. And — do I need the runtime to do this? No. [chuckles] The whole method runs on a transcript and a text file. You can audit your own last pitch tonight, in any editor.

tracks.title: Back up to the grammar
tracks.text: So — that's claims. A transcript is a source, not a document. The working document is the ledger you derive from it — every load-bearing sentence an org TODO whose state is its honesty, terminal only with cited evidence. And the gap between the talk and the build… is the backlog. [curious] This was a sub-lesson, under org — the grammar that lets a single line declare its own ladder of truth. If that line felt like magic, the way back up is short. Read org — the lesson on why a plan, or a pitch, can be checked at all. Everything the audit does… is built on that one idea.
